summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns from suitable inputs paired with desired outputs to improve an evaluated stable task or behavior. Full-weight tuning and supported LoRA are different ways to update weights during that learning.
clue: Consistent domain behavior with a demonstrated quality gain.
trap: Daily private-document refresh and citations are not implemented merely by changing weights.
capability: Supported Bedrock fine-tuning/customization or SageMaker adaptation plus independent evaluation and compatible serving.
example: For a case classifier, train on case text → approved category examples after defining the label boundary; test on independent cases rather than memorized training records.
managed: Eligible Bedrock customization or SageMaker jobs executes supported tuning/configuration contracts.
extension: Supply suitable approved labeled records or a compatible parameter-efficient method where supported.
ownership: Own data quality/splits, held-out benefit, artifact compatibility, approval, and deployment/rollback.
constraint: Tuning must address a measured stable gap and improve required held-out behavior enough to justify lifecycle cost.

title: Continued pre-training
summary: Continue an eligible existing model’s training on suitable unlabeled domain text. For text LLMs, self-supervised next-token prediction learns from the text itself; it does not require explicit question/ideal-answer pairs. This extends an existing model rather than training a new foundation model from scratch.
clue: Domain adaptation differs from supervised instruction examples.
trap: This option is model-specific and not a real-time source lookup.
capability: Model-specific continued pre-training where eligible; retrieval remains the separate current-source capability.
example: An approved technical corpus may help a model learn domain language. Compare held-out task results with the original baseline; later policy changes still need current evidence.
managed: Eligible Bedrock continued pre-training or a controlled SageMaker training path executes the supported method.
extension: Supply approved suitable domain text for the supported continued pre-training objective. This is often called domain-adaptive pre-training (DAPT); compare it with the unchanged baseline.
ownership: Own data approval, independent task evaluation, compatibility, lifecycle cost, and release support.
constraint: Verify method/model support and a measured domain benefit; do not treat weights as a live source lookup.

title: Datasets / splits
summary: Version approved training/tuning data and separate representative held-out evaluation data with source/tool references.
clue: Preserve expert labels and rare/critical cohorts.
trap: Tuning on the held-out final test invalidates its independence.
example: A perfect score on records copied from training does not establish behavior on a new customer case. Version and separate the data used for tuning and final acceptance.
managed: S3 stores approved versioned datasets; supported evaluation/training jobs consume their configured records. Those jobs do not independently establish that labels and splits represent your business task.
extension: Use Glue/Data Quality or application checks for explicit rules, duplicate/label review, quarantine, and sensitive-data handling before jobs consume records.
ownership: Own source approval, task labels, split independence, provenance, critical-cohort coverage, and test-set protection. Final held-out cases must not become tuning inputs.
capability: S3/version metadata records lineage; Glue/Data Quality supports explicit gates; Bedrock/SageMaker jobs uses supported record formats; experts/application checks validates task meaning.
constraint: Data must be approved, correctly labeled/formatted, representative, and separated into appropriate tuning and independent evaluation sets.

title: Evaluate / human gates
summary: Measure quality, correctness, faithfulness, safety, latency, and cost; use calibrated automated/judge checks and accountable human review where needed.
clue: Critical regression blocks promotion even when averages improve.
trap: Human review and automated evaluation complement each other; neither is automatically infallible.
capability: Bedrock evaluation measures eligible model/RAG qualities; deterministic/domain checks covers objective and high-risk requirements; Step Functions or a delivery pipeline enforces required promotion gates.
example: Before promoting a candidate, compare it with the accepted baseline on the same independent cases, including critical cohorts that an average could hide.
managed: Supported Bedrock evaluation executes eligible automated/judge/human comparisons; SageMaker/application workflows can run applicable checks. The evaluator does not decide your business release policy.
extension: Add source-fact assertions, valid tool outcomes, calibrated rubrics, human review, and quality/safety/performance thresholds appropriate to the candidate.
ownership: Own held-out references, judge calibration, cohort gates, approval authority, and acceptance/rollback criteria. Block a critical regression even when overall quality rises.
constraint: The actual intended release configuration must pass independent task, safety, and relevant latency/cost requirements before approval.

title: Deploy / invoke
summary: Release a compatible approved model/prompt/retrieval configuration with version attribution and rollback.
clue: Control serving infrastructure only when required.
trap: A registered artifact does not automatically update an endpoint.
example: A registry approval does not make a new adapter live. Deployment must load the compatible artifact, select its route, and pass an attributed smoke request.
managed: SageMaker endpoints/inference components or the configured Bedrock invocation path provide supported serving operations. Model Registry records eligible artifacts/approval, rather than automatically changing live routes.
extension: Compose explicit artifact promotion, canary/shadow/blue-green exposure where appropriate, version attribution, and smoke/rollback checks in the delivery workflow.
ownership: Own the approved model/base-adapter/template/settings combination, side-effect isolation, critical-cohort stop criteria, state compatibility, and tested rollback route.
capability: Registry → version/approval evidence. Serving deployment/router → actual invoked identity. Canary limits exposure; shadow isolates candidate output/side effects; blue-green switches prepared environments.
constraint: Release the evaluated compatible configuration safely, prove its live identity, and preserve a working compatible rollback target.

comparison.title: Which rollout answers the release question?
rows: Small exposure still has real effects
comparison.note: Evaluate and approve first. Verify the actual live model/adapter/prompt/configuration. Model Registry alone does not update an endpoint or hot-swap an adapter.

title: Capacity / routing
summary: Separate intermittent on-demand use, measured reserved capacity, and eligible cross-Region routing.
clue: Stable demand and approved processing destinations are different constraints.
trap: An inference profile does not independently fail over the source application or provide chosen GPU controls.
capability: On-demand for flexible eligible calls; Provisioned Throughput for measured supported reservation needs; profiles for eligible allowed routing, currently without Provisioned Throughput.
example: Intermittent demand, stable token throughput, and geographic compute routing are different requirements with different costs.
managed: Bedrock on-demand, supported Provisioned Throughput, and eligible inference profiles supply distinct serving/routing contracts.
extension: Size/evaluate supported options from measured workload and approved destinations; add appropriate application admission.
ownership: Own quotas/demand, cost comparison, tail-latency measurement, destination policy, and source-application recovery.
constraint: Capacity must meet real token demand within support, cost, latency, and geographic policy.

title: Monitor / improve
summary: Correlate production versions and outcomes, turn failures into regressions, and roll back critical degradation.
clue: Quality drift and failed tool outcomes need more than uptime metrics.
trap: A monitoring chart does not itself generate calibrated quality scores.
example: One tenant/task route can regress while endpoint uptime and aggregate latency look normal. Track outcomes by release and cohort, not health alone.
managed: CloudWatch supported metrics/logs and configured invocation/tool tracing captures emitted evidence. These services do not automatically judge business correctness or decide that retraining is required.
extension: Emit scoped outcome/cohort/version signals, add confirmed failures to the golden dataset, and trigger your evaluation/rollback process under explicit criteria.
ownership: Own attribution, drift/failure analysis, critical-cohort monitoring, regression updates, and release response. Diagnose data/context/route changes before choosing model adaptation.
capability: CloudWatch, protected invocation/application logs, and X-Ray/OTel/tool traces provide evidence; golden-dataset evaluation and deployment controls guide the response.
constraint: Monitor actual quality, safety, latency/cost, and actions for the invoked release; investigate or roll back critical degradation.

title: One bounded task → Lambda
summary: Run a bounded operation and externalize durable state. Split long waits into an appropriate workflow/job.
clue: Short stateless adapter, validation, or lookup.
trap: Warm execution memory is not a guaranteed persistent service lifecycle.
capability: Lambda for one bounded operation; Step Functions/SQS for appropriate durable coordination or buffering around it.
example: Run a bounded extraction/tool/API task; persist progress elsewhere when the overall job includes long waits.
managed: Lambda manages eligible function execution; a conventional invocation is limited to 15 minutes.
extension: Compose bounded functions with Step Functions or queued workers for the broader durable job.
ownership: Own side-effect validation, external state, deadlines, retries/idempotency, dependencies, and rate control.
constraint: The operation must fit the execution/runtime contract without using a function as a long-lived approval wait.

title: Known durable workflow → Step Functions
summary: Developers define states, retries, branches, and approval waits. Bounded Bedrock/tool tasks can sit inside the workflow.
clue: Known sequence + durable state + hours-long approval.
trap: Model-selected autonomy is not needed just because a process is complex.
managed: Step Functions executes explicit configured states, retries, branches, and applicable durable integration/wait contracts.
extension: Use Choice/Parallel/Map and supported Retry/Catch/callback patterns around bounded model/business tasks.
ownership: Define state/approval/deadline rules, protect callback identity, and keep external business effects idempotent.
capability: Standard supports eligible .sync/callback waits and long duration; Express has different duration/integration limits, including no callback task tokens.
example: A fixed review process must remember which step completed, wait for the authenticated decision, then branch on it.
constraint: Known workflow transitions, durable state, recovery, and waits must match the selected workflow type.

title: Agents / frameworks
summary: An agent uses a model to choose the next permitted action, observes the tool result, and repeats until an answer or stopping condition. Choose the control pattern first, then how to implement the loop and where to host it.
clue: The next tool cannot be expressed as a known fixed sequence.
trap: Framework/runtime choice does not supply business authorization.
capability: Strands and LangChain supply agent-loop abstractions; LangGraph supplies graph/state control. AgentCore Harness supplies a managed loop; AgentCore Runtime hosts compatible code-defined agents.
example: A diagnostic task chooses its next permitted tool from observations; a required refund approval still follows business policy.
managed: AgentCore Harness supplies and runs a configured agent loop. AgentCore Runtime supplies hosting for your code; a handwritten loop or framework remains your implementation responsibility.
extension: Configure an eligible managed harness with supported models, tools, and limits. When its contract does not fit, implement the needed loop or graph with compatible code or a framework.
ownership: Own tool authorization, business preconditions, approval rules, side-effect idempotency, and acceptance tests. Configure limits and recovery even when a library or service runs the loop.
constraint: Use dynamic tool selection only where the next action genuinely depends on observations, within enforced authority.

comparison.title: What makes this an agent?
rows: Model proposes; application checks and executes once
Tool calling alone ≠ continuing agent loop
Model chooses permitted action from observations
Approval and business rules remain enforced checkpoints
comparison.note: For “Why was my refund rejected?”, the agent may choose which records to inspect next. Issuing a refund still requires enforced ownership, policy, and approval checks.

additionalComparisons.title: How will you build the loop?
rows: Your code calls model / validates tools / repeats
Model-led tool use with configurable SDK control
Agent harness / model and tool integrations
Compose agent behavior with higher-level abstractions
Mix required steps with agentic investigation
Supported managed contract meets the requirement
Custom graph or hooks → assess code-based runtime
additionalComparisons.note: These are implementation choices, not five separate agent types or required wrappers. LangGraph can contain an agent loop. Hosting is separate: AgentCore Runtime can host your own or framework-based code; AgentCore Harness runs a managed loop inside Runtime. Every option still needs enforced business authorization.

sources.title: AI Agents: examples and deeper explanation

title: Decouple / buffer → Events / SQS
summary: EventBridge routes events to targets; SQS retains work for paced consumers. These can support ingestion or runtime jobs.
clue: Independent event consumers differ from a worker buffer under a fixed model rate.
trap: Queues do not automatically implement token-rate admission.
capability: EventBridge → independent event targets; SQS → durable buffering/paced workers. A shared worker queue distributes rather than broadcasts every job.
example: An event must reach independent targets, while bursts before a slow target need buffering and pacing.
managed: EventBridge routes configured events; SQS stores work for configured consumers/redelivery.
extension: Filter/rout events, put queues before constrained consumers, and compose appropriate workers/workflows.
ownership: Own delivery/retry/DLQ policy, idempotency, queue deadlines, and safe processing rate.
constraint: Match fan-out versus work distribution and keep accepted work recoverable under consumer demand/capacity.

title: Tool runtime / MCP hosting
summary: Match each tool’s duration, dependencies, connection lifecycle, and compute needs. Use a persistent service only when it is required.
clue: Long-lived compatible CPU service differs from a short DynamoDB lookup.
trap: External session state alone does not force every handler into containers.
capability: Lambda/ECS/Fargate/compatible AgentCore runtime according to execution needs; MCP connectivity does not establish exactly-once business completion.
example: A tool that times out may already have completed a write; inspect its authoritative outcome before another side-effecting attempt.
managed: Compatible tool runtimes hosts code under their duration/connection/dependency contract; MCP exposes the configured tool interface.
extension: Use bounded Lambda calls or an appropriate persistent ECS/Fargate/agent runtime only where the tool actually requires it.
ownership: Own tool authentication, scope, inputs, deadlines, outcome reconciliation, and idempotency.
constraint: The hosting and tool contract must fit runtime needs and provide evidence for safe business recovery.

title: Authentication / IAM
summary: Identify the caller and evaluate allowed AWS actions/resources using the applicable policies and explicit denies.
clue: Who is calling differs from which customer record they may use.
trap: An ingestion role’s source access is not every end user’s document permission.
capability: Cognito/federation for identity; IAM for AWS access; backend/data authorization for business records; CloudTrail coverage for API audit.
example: A signed-in user is identifiable but still needs permission for the requested document or transaction.
managed: Cognito/appropriate federation verifies identity; IAM evaluates applicable AWS action/resource policies and explicit denies.
extension: Carry the verified identity/role into backend entitlement checks and supported private/API integrations.
ownership: Own tenant/record/action mapping and caller attribution; do not treat an ingestion role as every user’s permission.
constraint: Establish the effective caller and applicable policy separately from permitted tenant/tool data scope.

title: Tenant isolation / retrieval filtering
summary: Derive scope from trusted identity; enforce permitted document access before context and business access before tool writes.
clue: Tenant A must never receive tenant B’s passages.
trap: A high similarity score or a Guardrail does not grant access.
managed: IAM and supported store/query integrations enforces their configured access contract; content filtering is a different capability.
extension: Derive scope from trusted identity, apply supported fail-closed metadata/access filters, and validate each business API action.
ownership: Own entitlement mapping, complete/correct access tags, denial tests, and bypass removal before context or writes.
capability: Backend authorization plus eligible Knowledge Bases filtering; IAM/S3 access controls; Lake Formation through integrated query paths, not independent direct S3 bypasses.
example: Tenant A must be denied Tenant B’s passage even when the passage is relevant and its wording passes safety filtering.
constraint: Only permitted records may enter the caller’s context or business action path.

title: KMS / encryption
summary: Protect source, intermediate, vector, result, state, and log copies with required encryption and key access.
clue: Inventory derived copies rather than protecting only original S3 objects.
trap: Encryption does not authorize a tenant or prove deletion.
capability: KMS/service encryption plus TLS; Secrets Manager for relevant credentials/secrets; application access/deletion policy remains separate.
example: Encrypting the source is insufficient if an extraction bucket or prompt log contains an unprotected sensitive copy.
managed: KMS and eligible service encryption configuration protects configured copies; TLS protects supported transport.
extension: Configure scoped key/service policies for source, index, intermediate, result, state, and log access.
ownership: Inventory derived copies, verify protection and required key use, and keep entitlement/location/retention separate.
constraint: Every required copy/path must meet encryption and scoped key-use policy without granting excessive access.

title: VPC / PrivateLink
summary: Use eligible interface endpoints, private DNS, endpoint policies, and network controls for the required private API path.
clue: API traffic must stay on the approved private path.
trap: A private subnet alone is not a private service endpoint.
capability: Supported interface endpoints/PrivateLink plus private DNS/network/endpoint/IAM policy for the selected service.
example: Private subnets alone do not prove that the invoked service endpoint resolves and routes over the required private path.
managed: Eligible interface VPC endpoints/PrivateLink provide supported private service access when configured.
extension: Set applicable private DNS, routing/network controls, endpoint policy, and scoped IAM access.
ownership: Verify the actual request path, remove bypass routes, and test entitlement/residency independently.
constraint: Use the actual approved private API path, not an assumption based on workload subnet placement.

title: Guardrails / content safety
summary: Apply supported content, sensitive-information, and grounding policies at the interaction stages they cover.
clue: Harmful content and unsupported claims need the appropriate safety check.
trap: Guardrails is not authorization or a guarantee against every indirect/tool-result injection.
capability: Bedrock Guardrails for eligible content checks; source/query/response grounding only for supported use cases, excluding conversational QA/chatbot; backend authorization remains separate.
example: A safe displayed sentence can coexist with an unauthorized document in context or an invalid business write.
managed: Guardrails applies supported configured content, sensitive-information, prompt-attack, and grounding policies within their documented limits.
extension: Apply the relevant supported checks at input/output boundaries and combine them with deterministic task/access checks.
ownership: Own policy selection, untrusted-source handling, fallback, entitlement, and action authorization; test indirect/tool-result paths explicitly.
constraint: Use the correct safety policy at its supported boundary without substituting it for data/tool permission.

title: PII / sensitive copies
summary: Locate where PII exists, choose discovery/detection/filtering for that location, and verify required transformation/retention.
clue: S3 discovery → Macie; supported text pipeline → Comprehend; model interaction → Guardrails.
trap: Detecting sensitive spans does not sanitize every index, log, or backup.
capability: Macie → S3 discovery; Comprehend → text detection; Guardrails → eligible model I/O policy; application/pipeline transformation verifies sanitization.
example: A PII detection job is not a successful redaction job if the original identifier is still embedded or logged.
managed: Macie discovers supported S3 sensitive data; Comprehend detects supported text spans; Guardrails handles eligible model-interaction policies.
extension: Apply and verify required masking/redaction before downstream copies; enforce failure/quarantine when transformation is incomplete.
ownership: Own the sensitive-data inventory, transformation verification, access/retention, and derived-copy tests.
constraint: Identify where sensitive data exists and verify the required handling on actual downstream bytes/copies.

title: Permission ceilings / residency / retention
summary: Use applicable organizational/identity ceilings and approved processing destinations; manage retention and deletion of derived copies.
clue: Local IAM allow cannot override an applicable explicit SCP deny.
trap: Permission ceilings do not grant access; private encrypted transport does not establish residency.
capability: IAM/SCP ceilings, approved in-Region/eligible profile routing, and each source/index/cache/log retention/deletion configuration protects different requirements.
example: A source deletion must reach its chunks, vectors, caches, and retained outputs; private transport does not authorize another Region.
managed: SCPs/permissions boundaries limits applicable permissions; eligible routing/storage services follows their configured destination/retention contracts.
extension: Configure allowed destinations, copy-specific retention/update/delete, and explicit source/cache/index synchronization.
ownership: Own policy interpretation, copy inventory, bypass removal, exact model/endpoint retention support, and lifecycle verification.
constraint: Enforce permitted locations, applicable permission ceilings, and lifecycle rules across original and derived copies.

title: Recall / precision
summary: Recall assesses required-evidence coverage; precision/relevance assesses retrieval noise. Inspect actual candidates/context as well as scores.
clue: Missing relevant passage differs from too many irrelevant passages.
trap: Good retrieval does not guarantee faithful generation.
example: The correct exception is absent from the candidate set, while several unrelated policy pages are returned. Measure evidence coverage and noise separately before changing the answer prompt.
managed: Knowledge Bases and its supported store execute retrieval; evaluation records whether required passages appeared. Retrieval success alone does not prove that the model used them faithfully.
extension: Compare supported search modes, filters, candidate counts, and reranking on the same representative questions. Change ingestion when the missing passage was never indexed.
ownership: Define expected evidence per question, inspect actual candidate/context content, and measure recall alongside relevance. Keep permissions and source versions consistent across comparisons.
capability: Knowledge Bases Retrieve exposes candidates; supported vector/lexical/hybrid search and reranking address different retrieval boundaries. A golden dataset supplies the expected evidence.
constraint: Required evidence must reach the permitted candidate set without overwhelming context with irrelevant passages.

title: Correctness / faithfulness / relevance
summary: Correctness compares with references, faithfulness checks source support, and relevance checks whether the response answers the question.
clue: Correct evidence with an unsupported claim → faithfulness/context-use investigation.
trap: A real citation or valid JSON does not prove source support.
example: An answer cites the correct refund policy but invents a guarantee the passage never makes. The citation exists; the additional claim still lacks evidence.
managed: Eligible Bedrock evaluation capabilities run supported evaluations. A model judge supplies a judgment under its configured rubric; it does not replace an authoritative reference or business rule.
extension: Use task-specific rubrics and supported custom metrics, with deterministic checks for objective contracts and calibrated human review for ambiguous judgments.
ownership: Define correctness, source support, and relevance separately. Retain the question, evidence, response, and expected outcome so a good score can be challenged.
capability: Bedrock evaluation where supported; deterministic application checks; calibrated human review. Grounding checks require their supported source/query/response contract.
constraint: An answer must solve the task, stay supported by evidence, and address the actual question; these are separate tests.

title: Automated / judge / human
summary: Use deterministic checks for objective contracts, calibrated judges for semantic scale, and experts for labels/high-risk nuance.
clue: Thousands of rubric-scored answers with a limited expert sample → calibrated judge plus targeted human review.
trap: BLEU/ROUGE overlap is not semantic truth; judge scores can be biased or wrong.
example: A release produces valid JSON but chooses the wrong contract category. Schema validation passes, while reference-label checks fail; an open-ended quality judge addresses a different question.
managed: Bedrock evaluation supports eligible automated/model-judge and human workflows. Each evaluator measures its configured task; no single score proves every contract.
extension: Add deterministic field/action checks and supported task-specific evaluation criteria. Calibrate judge results against labeled examples and human decisions.
ownership: Own the rubric, reference quality, judge calibration, critical cohorts, and release thresholds. Use reviewers when the outcome cannot be settled by an objective check.
capability: Bedrock evaluation for supported quality tasks; application validators for schemas and business rules; human evaluation for nuanced or consequential cases.
constraint: Choose an evaluator that can actually test the required outcome, then verify agreement on representative examples.

title: Safety / latency / cost
summary: Assess critical cohorts, actual tool outcomes, first-token/total/queue latency, and tokens/cost per successful outcome.
clue: Faster first text differs from lower total generation time.
trap: The cheapest invocation can be expensive per successful task if it fails or retries.
example: Users see the first token quickly, but a long queue and repeated failed calls make the task slow and expensive. Measure the whole successful interaction.
managed: CloudWatch exposes available service metrics; instrumented application traces attribute queue, retrieval, model, and transport time. Billing tools describe cost, not every request’s bottleneck.
extension: Emit stage timing, token counts, retries, and outcome metrics. Compare eligible inference modes or capacity changes using the same workload and quality gate.
ownership: Define first-token and completion targets separately, inspect latency distributions, and calculate cost per successful task including retries and failed attempts.
capability: CloudWatch metrics/alarms and X-Ray/OpenTelemetry spans locate operational bottlenecks; eligible Bedrock inference modes address a measured capacity or delivery requirement.
constraint: Meet measured end-to-end latency and cost targets without sacrificing the required quality or success rate.

title: Repeated work / caching
summary: Identify the reusable unit: exact scoped result, semantically equivalent answer, or supported identical prompt prefix.
clue: Stable system prefix with new answers → prompt caching.
trap: A prompt cache is not response reuse; response cache keys must include scope and version.
capability: Bedrock prompt caching for eligible repeated prefixes; scoped application result caches for reusable answers. Choose by the unit of work being reused.
example: Two users ask the same words but have different document permissions. Reusing one complete answer across both is unsafe even when the text looks equivalent.
managed: Eligible Bedrock prompt caching reuses supported identical prompt prefixes. It does not return a previously generated application answer.
extension: An application result cache can reuse exact or semantically equivalent answers only when the complete scoped inputs and freshness rules make reuse valid.
ownership: Own tenant/access isolation, input/configuration/version identity, expiry, and invalidation. Measure whether the answer remains valid before adopting semantic result reuse.
constraint: Only reuse work whose input, permission scope, configuration, and freshness remain valid for the new request.

comparison.title: What exactly can be reused?
rows: Reuses prompt work, not a stored answer
comparison.note: Define the reusable unit before choosing a cache. Compare measured savings with stale-answer, access-scope, and quality risks.

title: Release / rollout
summary: Offline gates precede controlled exposure. Canary limits live exposure; A/B compares live outcomes; shadow compares isolated copied requests.
clue: Candidate output must not reach users and writes must not occur → isolated shadow.
trap: Hiding the candidate answer does not suppress production tool side effects.
example: A candidate is ready for live comparison, but its refund tool could still write production records. Hiding its answer is insufficient to make shadow traffic safe.
managed: Supported deployment/routing capabilities provide configured traffic exposure. They do not decide whether candidate tools may write or whether a cohort regression is acceptable.
extension: Use canary for limited exposure, A/B for live outcome comparison, isolated shadow for copied requests, or blue/green for a controlled switch with rollback.
ownership: Own offline approval gates, side-effect isolation, cohort thresholds, release identity, and a verified rollback target. Stop promotion when a critical cohort fails.
capability: Eligible SageMaker deployment/traffic controls and application routing implement the selected rollout pattern; CloudWatch and evaluation signals inform rollback.
constraint: Expose the candidate in the required way while containing side effects and preserving a compatible rollback release.

comparison.title: Which rollout answers the release question?
rows: Small exposure still has real effects
comparison.note: Evaluate and approve first. Verify the actual live model/adapter/prompt/configuration. Model Registry alone does not update an endpoint or hot-swap an adapter.

title: Review / diagnose
summary: Review a whole path forward to understand its responsibilities. Choose an observed symptom to investigate backwards through earlier boundaries.
clue: Find the first demonstrated inconsistency using versioned inputs, metrics, traces, and actual outputs.
trap: Do not debug training loss for a routing defect, rerank an absent chunk, or use Guardrails as tenant authorization.
example: A correct passage was indexed but never entered the candidates. Start from the observed answer and trace evidence backward; changing the training loss cannot repair this retrieval defect.
managed: Managed services expose supported job status, retrieval output, inference metrics, and logs. Those records provide evidence for diagnosis, not an automatic root-cause verdict.
extension: Instrument missing boundaries and run controlled comparisons using the same question, identity, data version, prompt, and model configuration.
ownership: Find the first demonstrated mismatch, distinguish upstream absence from downstream misuse, and verify the proposed fix on the original failing cases.
capability: Knowledge Bases retrieval output, CloudWatch, invocation/application logs, X-Ray/OpenTelemetry, and evaluation cases reveal different portions of the path.
constraint: Locate the responsibility that first fails its contract before choosing a service, extension, or custom change.

title: CloudWatch metrics / alarms
summary: Track token counts, latency distributions, throttles/errors, queue age, and emitted quality/outcome signals.
clue: Operational threshold on InputTokenCount → metric alarm.
trap: Cost Explorer analyzes billing and Budgets alerts; neither is this runtime metric alarm.
capability: CloudWatch metrics and alarms for runtime signals; Cost Explorer for billing analysis; AWS Budgets for configured budget alerts.
example: A token-volume alarm must fire during a burst. A later billing alert may help manage spend, but cannot substitute for the requested runtime signal.
managed: CloudWatch stores available service/custom metrics, evaluates configured alarms, and exposes operational trends. It cannot infer a business-quality signal that the application never emits.
extension: Add scoped custom outcome/quality signals and stage timing when built-in metrics do not cover the requirement.
ownership: Choose thresholds, dimensions, aggregation windows, and an actionable response. Correlate alarms with request/release identity rather than treating an average as universal.
constraint: Use the signal and time window that match the operational requirement, including critical cohorts and tail behavior.

title: CloudTrail caller audit
summary: Record required AWS API activity with the appropriate event coverage; correlate caller, time, and operation.
clue: Who invoked or changed an AWS resource?
trap: Caller audit events are not the complete model input/output record.
capability: AWS CloudTrail for caller/API audit; Bedrock invocation logging and application logs when permitted interaction content is also required.
example: An investigator needs to identify who changed the inference configuration. The caller, operation, and timestamp are audit evidence; the complete prompt is a separate logging need.
managed: CloudTrail records AWS API activity under the configured event coverage and selectors. Audit records are distinct from model interaction-content logs.
extension: Configure the required event coverage and correlate events with application request/release identifiers where available.
ownership: Own coverage verification, retention, access, and correlation. Do not promise complete prompt/answer evidence from caller audit events.
constraint: Capture the required caller/resource changes with appropriate event coverage and protected retention.

title: Invocation / application logging
summary: Explicitly enable supported interaction-content logging where policy allows; protect destinations, retention, and sensitive inputs.
clue: Need the actual prompt and answer rather than only the caller.
trap: Logging is not enabled by assuming CloudTrail; logs can retain sensitive pre-masking input.
capability: Bedrock Model Invocation Logging to CloudWatch Logs/S3 where supported and allowed; application logs for request/tool context; KMS and access controls protect destinations.
example: The response masks an identifier, but an earlier prompt log still contains it. Inspect the stored input and logging point instead of assuming output redaction protected every copy.
managed: Explicitly configured Bedrock invocation logging records supported interaction content to protected destinations. CloudTrail caller audit does not enable this content record.
extension: Add scoped application/tool logs where the service record omits needed context; redact before persistence when the policy requires it.
ownership: Own sensitive-input handling, permissions, retention, deletion, and destination protection. Check actual stored bytes, including content captured before masking.
constraint: Keep sufficient diagnostic evidence without persisting content that violates the application’s privacy or retention requirements.

title: Spans / agent / tool traces
summary: Instrument retrieval, model, and tool boundaries; retain relevant workflow/agent events and correlate them with request/version identity.
clue: Which stage consumed eight seconds or caused the tool failure?
trap: Uninstrumented stages and hidden model internals do not automatically become visible.
capability: X-Ray/OpenTelemetry for instrumented stage spans; supported agent traces, Step Functions history, and tool logs for their respective execution evidence.
example: A request takes eight seconds, but the model call takes one. Spans around retrieval, queueing, and tools can locate the remaining delay; a total timer cannot.
managed: X-Ray/OpenTelemetry tooling handles emitted trace data; supported agent traces and workflow history expose their recorded events. Uninstrumented stages remain gaps.
extension: Instrument retrieval, context assembly, model, transport, and tool boundaries; propagate correlation identifiers through asynchronous work.
ownership: Own useful span boundaries, safe metadata, request/version attribution, and interpretation. Hidden model internals do not become visible merely by enabling tracing.
constraint: Attribute latency or failure to the actual responsibility with correlated evidence across the full request path.

title: Training records / task format
summary: Validate model-specific schemas, input/output alignment, labels, duplicate examples, and cohort coverage before a training job.
clue: Clean task examples matter more than raw record count.
trap: A successful schema check does not prove label correctness or prevent data leakage.
capability: S3 datasets, Glue/Data Quality, and selected Bedrock customization or SageMaker training input validation cover storage, preparation, and format boundaries.
example: Two nearly identical support messages have different reference labels, and a copied example appears in validation. A valid file format will not reveal either semantic defect.
managed: S3 stores approved datasets; Glue and supported quality rules prepare/check records. The selected customization or training service validates its required input format.
extension: Add model-specific schema, label-alignment, duplicate/leakage, and cohort checks before starting the training job.
ownership: Own label definitions, correct targets, independent splits, and representative coverage. Fail or quarantine invalid records instead of merely producing a report.
constraint: Training examples must be correctly supervised, compatible with the selected method, and separated from independent evaluation cases.

title: Training configuration
summary: Verify the supported base model/method, tokenizer and sequence format, learning rate, epochs, batch configuration, and available compute.
clue: Loss diverges after a learning-rate change → inspect the training configuration and data.
trap: More epochs or a higher learning rate is not a universal fix.
capability: Eligible Bedrock customization settings or SageMaker training configuration; job logs/metrics and held-out evaluation determine whether a change helped.
example: A previously stable job diverges after a learning-rate change. Compare the actual dataset and configuration rather than assuming more epochs will improve the model.
managed: Eligible Bedrock customization exposes supported settings; SageMaker training provides the configured training environment and job execution under its contract.
extension: Adjust supported learning rate, epochs, batch/sequence settings, or training implementation where permitted; change one hypothesis at a time.
ownership: Own method/base compatibility, tokenizer/task format, configuration versions, and representative validation. Choose settings from measured behavior rather than a universal recipe.
constraint: The training configuration must fit the supported model/method and improve the required held-out task without instability.

title: Training / validation curves
summary: Compare available training and validation metrics over time, plus held-out task outputs; retain the job, dataset, configuration, and checkpoint versions.
clue: Training improves while held-out behavior worsens → investigate generalization, leakage, and overfitting.
trap: Low training loss is not proof of useful or safe production behavior.
capability: Available Bedrock customization metrics or SageMaker training logs/metrics, plus task evaluation, separate fit to training data from useful generalization.
example: Training loss falls each epoch, but held-out classification gets worse. The model is fitting its training examples; production usefulness has not been established.
managed: Bedrock customization exposes available output metrics; SageMaker training records configured logs/metrics. Availability depends on the selected job/method.
extension: Compare training and validation curves with held-out task outputs, and inspect data/configuration changes when the trends disagree.
ownership: Own independent evaluation, cohort analysis, and complete job/dataset/configuration lineage. Do not promote based only on the lowest training loss.
constraint: Training progress must translate into better independent task behavior, including the critical cohorts used for promotion.

title: Checkpoint / generalization
summary: Choose an artifact using independent task evaluation and critical-cohort gates, not merely the final epoch or lowest training loss.
clue: Original model beats the tuned candidate on held-out tasks → stop promotion and inspect the adaptation/data.
trap: A final training checkpoint is not automatically the best release.
example: The last checkpoint has the lowest training loss but fails rare contract exceptions. An earlier candidate or the baseline may be the safer release.
managed: Supported training workflows produce their artifacts/checkpoints; evaluation tooling measures configured tasks. Neither automatically selects the best business release.
extension: Compare available candidate artifacts against the same independent baseline and critical-cohort tests before approval.
ownership: Own artifact identity, held-out references, promotion thresholds, and rejection of regressions. Retain enough lineage to reproduce the comparison.
capability: Eligible Bedrock/SageMaker customization artifacts and supported evaluation workflows; SageMaker Model Registry can record the approved package and evidence.
constraint: Choose the evaluated artifact that meets release criteria, rather than automatically choosing the final epoch.

title: LoRA / parameter-efficient tuning
summary: LoRA is a parameter-efficient weight-update technique commonly used for fine-tuning: train low-rank adapter weights while the base stays frozen. SFT describes the learning objective; LoRA describes how weights change. An unmerged adapter needs its compatible base at inference.
clue: Task adaptation with a smaller trainable artifact → evaluate supported LoRA.
trap: LoRA is a fine-tuning technique, not RAG, a standalone foundation model, or a guarantee of higher quality.
managed: Eligible SageMaker training/serving capabilities support compatible adapter workflows. The selected model/runtime contract determines which adapter format and integration are supported.
extension: Use supported low-rank adapter training and serving integration. Keep retrieval for changing facts and evaluate prompting before deciding that weight adaptation is needed.
ownership: Own good supervision, compatible base/adapter/tokenizer versions, held-out evaluation, and deployment routing. A smaller trainable artifact does not remove those obligations.
capability: Supported LoRA training and compatible SageMaker adapter inference components where applicable; evaluate the exact base-plus-adapter serving pair.
example: A support-classification task needs stable behavior adaptation. A small LoRA artifact can encode that adaptation, but an unmerged adapter still requires its compatible base at inference.
constraint: Use a supported adapter workflow only when measured stable-task adaptation justifies it and the compatible pair can be served safely.

title: Rank / scaling / dropout
summary: Rank changes adapter capacity and resource use; scaling and dropout alter the training behavior. Tune with representative validation rather than a universal setting.
clue: Insufficient adaptation capacity differs from memorization or bad labels.
trap: Increasing rank does not repair wrong supervision and does not always improve generalization.
example: An adapter misses difficult categories, so the team raises rank. That changes capacity and resource use, but conflicting labels may still be the real limitation.
managed: The selected supported adapter-training implementation applies its rank, scaling, and dropout settings. Managed job execution does not determine the best values.
extension: Compare supported settings with fixed data and representative validation, separating insufficient capacity from memorization or bad supervision.
ownership: Own controlled experiments, label quality, resource measurements, and cohort results. Avoid assuming that increasing rank always improves generalization.
capability: Supported LoRA training configuration and training/validation metrics; independent task evaluation measures the benefit of rank/scaling/dropout choices.
constraint: Choose adapter settings that improve the required held-out behavior within resource limits, after checking supervision quality.

title: Adapter / base compatibility
summary: Track the exact base revision, adapter artifact, tokenizer/template, and supported serving format together. Check whether the adapter is merged or separately loaded.
clue: Small adapter file exists, but the request behaves like the base → check loading and routing.
trap: An adapter is not a complete model; matching a model-family name alone is insufficient.
example: A file is labeled with the right model family, yet loading fails or the output resembles the base. Verify exact revisions, format, tokenizer, and actual loading state.
managed: Compatible SageMaker serving capabilities load artifacts under their runtime contract. An adapter file alone is not a complete foundation model.
extension: Use the supported separately loaded adapter or merged-model path as appropriate; verify format and compatibility rather than assuming interchangeable deployment methods.
ownership: Own the exact base revision, adapter artifact, tokenizer/template, serving format, and evaluated pair. Test that the live request really invokes it.
capability: Compatible SageMaker adapter inference components or supported container serving; artifact/version records establish the deployed base-plus-adapter identity.
constraint: The adapter must match its exact base and serving contract, and the actual request must reach the evaluated pair.

title: Version / approval / Model Registry
summary: Record approved versioned artifacts, metrics, lineage, and rollback targets. Keep approval separate from the explicit deployment action.
clue: Approved model package, unchanged live output → inspect endpoint deployment and request routing.
trap: Model Registry approval does not update an endpoint or load a LoRA adapter.
capability: SageMaker Model Registry for package/version approval; an explicit deployment workflow and eligible endpoint/component operations for live serving changes.
example: A model package is approved, but users still receive the old behavior. Approval records a release decision; the serving route still needs an explicit deployment action.
managed: SageMaker Model Registry records versioned packages, approval, and associated metadata. Registry state does not update an endpoint or load a LoRA adapter.
extension: Connect approval to a governed deployment workflow that creates/updates the supported serving resources and verifies the intended route.
ownership: Own complete release lineage, evaluation evidence, deployment authorization, and a compatible rollback target. Verify live version identity after promotion.
constraint: Approval and live deployment must be separate, auditable actions tied to the same evaluated release.

title: LoRA serving / adapter routing
summary: Deploy the compatible base and selected adapter through a supported runtime. Verify the adapter identity actually invoked, loading status, authorization, and version attribution.
clue: Multiple task adapters share a base, but one tenant gets the wrong behavior → inspect adapter routing and access.
trap: Generic endpoint updates, merged-model releases, and adapter inference components have different deployment contracts.
capability: SageMaker adapter inference components where compatible, or supported container adapter serving; application authorization and route checks ensure the intended pair is invoked.
example: Two tenants share a base model but require different task adapters. If one sees the other’s behavior, inspect adapter routing and entitlement before retraining.
managed: Compatible SageMaker adapter inference components or supported container runtimes serve the configured base/adapter pair under their deployment contract.
extension: Use supported adapter loading/routing integration; distinguish separately loaded adapters from merged-model releases and ordinary endpoint updates.
ownership: Own authorized routing, compatibility, readiness checks, release attribution, and coherent rollback. Test the real application request, not only a direct component call.
constraint: Serve the correct authorized adapter/base pair and verify its identity through the actual production route.

title: Verify live release / rollback
summary: Check actual endpoint/component readiness and send a version-attributed smoke request through the real application route. Verify rollback restores a compatible full release.
clue: Offline candidate passes but live behavior is old → inspect deployed identity and route.
trap: Artifact registration or a completed update request is not proof that the intended version serves users.
example: The candidate passed offline tests, but a smoke request through the application returns the old version. Inspect endpoint/component readiness and routing, not the approval badge.
managed: The hosting service exposes supported deployment/readiness state. A completed update request or registered artifact is not proof of the version reached by users.
extension: Add version-attributed smoke checks and controlled rollback verification to the deployment workflow.
ownership: Own real-route tests, identity correlation, critical behavior checks, and restoration of a compatible full release, including dependent prompts/adapters/configuration.
capability: Eligible SageMaker endpoint/component status and deployment operations; application smoke requests, logs, and routing checks verify the live release.
constraint: The intended evaluated release must serve the real application path, and rollback must restore a compatible working release.

title: Generation / context configuration
summary: Check actual token limits, stop sequences, sampling configuration, supported API fields, tokenizer/template, and context truncation.
clue: Answer cuts off or differs from evaluation → inspect the actual inference payload/configuration.
trap: Lower temperature does not repair missing knowledge, a wrong adapter, or lost context.
example: The evaluated answer was complete, but production stops midway through a JSON object. Compare the live token limit, stop sequence, prompt/template, and context truncation.
managed: Bedrock or the selected SageMaker runtime applies supported inference parameters. Field names and supported controls depend on the chosen model/API.
extension: Adjust supported generation/context settings and application context assembly, then rerun the same quality and completeness tests.
ownership: Own the actual request payload, tokenizer/template, truncation policy, output validation, and configuration/version parity between evaluation and production.
capability: Bedrock Converse or supported model invocation fields; configured SageMaker inference parameters; application validators check the resulting contract.
constraint: The actual invocation must preserve necessary context and use supported settings that meet completeness and quality requirements.

title: Quantization / serving fit
summary: Reduce weight precision where the model/runtime supports it; measure memory, latency, and critical task quality on the target serving configuration.
clue: A memory footprint requirement points to serving/model representation, not chunk size.
trap: Smaller weights are not automatically faster or equally accurate; adapter/runtime compatibility still matters.
capability: Compatible SageMaker hosting/runtime configuration for supported quantization; measured endpoint benchmarks and held-out task evaluation establish serving fit.
example: A model no longer fits the target memory budget. Lower weight precision may help, but benchmark the actual runtime and rare-task quality before approving the smaller representation.
managed: The chosen compatible hosting/runtime executes supported quantized representations. Reduced weight size does not guarantee lower latency or equal accuracy.
extension: Use a supported quantization/runtime path and compare memory, latency, and quality on the intended serving configuration.
ownership: Own compatibility checks, critical-cohort gates, endpoint benchmarks, and rollback to an evaluated representation. Verify adapter support if the release uses one.
constraint: Meet the memory/serving requirement without assuming that smaller weights preserve speed, accuracy, or adapter compatibility.

title: Distillation
summary: Transfer teacher behavior to an eligible smaller student for a defined task. Bedrock uses generated or existing teacher responses to fine-tune the student; this is response-based distillation and can include supervised fine-tuning.
clue: Reduce serving cost for a defined task while preserving measured quality.
trap: Distillation is different from quantizing the same model or attaching a LoRA adapter.
capability: Eligible Bedrock distillation or SageMaker training; automated and human evaluation where appropriate test the smaller student’s task behavior.
example: A smaller student copies common teacher responses well but fails a rare policy exception. The lower serving cost cannot compensate for breaking a critical acceptance case.
managed: Eligible Bedrock distillation or a controlled SageMaker workflow trains a student under the selected supported contract. Eligibility and task fit must be checked.
extension: Use representative teacher/task prompts and supported synthetic-data generation or response reuse, then train the student. Compare the student and accepted teacher/baseline on independent critical cohorts.
ownership: Own dataset quality, held-out quality/latency/cost gates, critical-cohort acceptance, and a rollback release. Reject average gains that hide consequential failures.
constraint: Reduce measured serving cost/latency while preserving the defined task quality, including critical cohorts.

title: Token admission / queueing
summary: Inspect accepted request/token volume, queue age, timeouts, quotas, and team scope; pace accepted work against the real model capacity.
clue: 429s or long queue waits under bursts → examine admission and capacity before tuning prompts.
trap: API request throttles, worker concurrency, and billing alerts are not interchangeable token-budget controls.
example: A burst is accepted immediately, but workers issue too many model tokens and requests time out in the queue. Separate admission policy from actual downstream capacity.
managed: API Gateway handles configured request controls; SQS buffers accepted work; workers and model services operate within their configured capacity/quotas.
extension: Add scoped token/request admission, queue-age limits, and paced worker consumption appropriate to the workload.
ownership: Own token accounting, fairness, accepted-work semantics, timeout/rejection behavior, and capacity measurements. Billing alerts do not enforce a runtime token budget.
capability: API Gateway for request admission, SQS for decoupled backlog, bounded worker concurrency, and CloudWatch for queue/throttle signals; model capacity remains a separate limit.
constraint: Accept and pace only the work the downstream system can complete within its latency, quota, and team-scope requirements.

title: Tool arguments / business validation
summary: Inspect the chosen tool and its parameters, caller scope, preconditions, approvals, and authoritative outcome. Reject invalid writes before execution.
clue: Valid JSON but unauthorized or invalid action → deterministic authorization/business validation.
trap: Schema conformance is not permission or transaction correctness.
example: The model produces schema-valid refund arguments for a customer who is not eligible. The tool must reject the write before execution, regardless of fluent reasoning.
managed: Eligible agent/tool integrations carry structured calls; IAM and service permissions limit supported operations. Schema validation does not establish business entitlement.
extension: Place deterministic authorization, precondition checks, and required approval in the tool execution path before side effects.
ownership: Own caller scope, transaction rules, authoritative result checks, and refusal of invalid writes. Never treat the model’s claim of success as the business record.
capability: Agent tool/action integration plus IAM and application authorization; Lambda or suitable tool hosting applies deterministic business validation; Step Functions handles required durable approval.
constraint: Every proposed action must be authorized and satisfy business preconditions before a side effect executes.

title: Retries / idempotency / reconciliation
summary: Correlate retries and duplicate deliveries with durable work identity, execution state, DLQs, and the authoritative business record.
clue: Timeout followed by duplicate payment → inspect idempotency and result reconciliation.
trap: A model response or queue acknowledgment does not prove a side effect completed exactly once.
example: A payment call times out after the provider committed it. Blindly retrying creates a second payment; first reconcile the durable work identity with the authoritative outcome.
managed: SQS and event delivery expose their delivery/retry contracts; Step Functions manages configured workflow state and retries. These do not guarantee exactly-once business effects.
extension: Add durable idempotency, bounded retries, DLQ handling, and outcome reconciliation at the side-effect boundary.
ownership: Own work identity, transaction status, duplicate prevention, compensation where required, and the final user-visible result. Acknowledgment is not proof of completed work.
capability: SQS/EventBridge for decoupled delivery, Step Functions for explicit recovery state, and application idempotency/reconciliation against the authoritative business record.
constraint: Recover failed or uncertain work without duplicating side effects or claiming an unverified completion.
